record.question:
A law firm wants employees to use existing Active Directory credentials to access legal documents in S3. The firm already operates a trusted SAML 2.0 identity provider. Each employee must be able to list and access only that employee's assigned object prefix. The solution must avoid creating long-lived AWS credentials for employees. No other policies grant access to the bucket.

Which actions should the architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure SAML federation to an IAM role so employees obtain temporary AWS credentials. Have the trusted identity provider supply a protected, unique employee identifier as a session tag.

Use the trusted employee session tag in the role's S3 policy. Restrict ListBucket with an s3:prefix condition and restrict object actions to that employee's prefix ARN. Prevent employees from choosing or overriding another employee's identifier.
Grant the federated role access to every object in the bucket and hide other employees' folders in the client interface.
Create an IAM user and access key for every employee, and synchronize their IAM console passwords with Active Directory.
Create one shared IAM user for the application and distribute its access keys to all employees, using separate S3 folder names for organization.

explanation.text:
<<1>> and <<2>> are correct. Federation exchanges trusted SAML authentication for temporary role credentials. The role can use a trusted session tag to scope each employee's S3 requests without creating a separate IAM user or long-lived access key.

Two policy scopes are required: `s3:ListBucket` applies to the bucket ARN with an allowed-prefix condition, while object actions such as `s3:GetObject` and `s3:PutObject` apply to object ARNs under that prefix. Configure the role's SAML trust and required `sts:TagSession` permission, and ensure the identity provider controls the employee identifier. A user-selectable prefix tag would defeat isolation.

<<3>> provides interface filtering, not authorization; direct API calls would retain broad access.

<<4>> introduces long-lived AWS identities and credentials instead of federation.

<<5>> loses per-user isolation and distributes a shared long-lived secret.

Do not copy a policy using `${aws:username}` into this federated-role design: that variable is not available for IAM role sessions. Use an appropriate trusted identity attribute.

Official AWS references (checked September 18, 2026): [STS session tags](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_session-tags.html). [S3 home-prefix policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_examples_s3_home-directory-console.html).

diagram_alt: Trusted federation attributes scope both S3 listing and object permissions, rather than relying on folder names or client-side hiding.

sources.supports: SAML principal tags, role trust requirements, and principal-tag authorization
Bucket-prefix versus object-resource permissions and aws:username absence for IAM roles

editorial_notes: Preserved answer set 1 and 2. Replaced legacy directory synchronization with SAML role federation and a protected session-tag prefix, explicitly avoiding aws:username for role sessions.
